# Manufacturing Method for Three-Dimensional Shaped Objects with Enhanced Heat Removal Properties

## Overview and Purpose

The present manufacturing method is directed toward producing a three-dimensional shaped object specifically designed for use as a metal mold, with particular emphasis on achieving superior heat removal characteristics. This objective is accomplished through a precisely controlled additive manufacturing process that enables the creation of complex internal geometries not achievable through conventional mold-making techniques. By optimizing the internal structure of the mold, the resulting product can more efficiently dissipate heat during the molding process, thereby improving cycle times, product quality, and overall manufacturing efficiency.

## Fundamental Process Methodology

The core of this manufacturing method relies on an iterative, layer-by-layer construction approach that alternates between two fundamental steps: powder-layer formation and solidified-layer formation. This cyclical process is repeated multiple times in succession, with each cycle contributing an additional layer to the gradually developing three-dimensional structure. Through this systematic repetition, the object is built incrementally from the bottom up, allowing for precise control over both the external geometry and internal features of the final shaped object.

## Solidified-Layer Formation Process

During each cycle, a solidified layer is generated through a controlled irradiation process. Specifically, a light beam—which may take the form of a laser or other suitable high-energy source—is directed onto predetermined portions of a freshly formed powder layer. The energy delivered by this light beam induces localized heating sufficient to cause either sintering or melting of the powder material at the targeted locations. Upon subsequent cooling, the affected powder solidifies into a cohesive layer, effectively transforming loose powder particles into a solid, structurally integrated section of the object. The selective nature of this irradiation process, wherein only specific portions of the powder layer are targeted, allows the geometry of each layer to be finely controlled according to the design specifications of the three-dimensional object.

## Sequential Layer Building

Following the formation of each solidified layer, the manufacturing process advances by depositing a new layer of powder directly on top of the previously solidified layer. This newly formed powder layer is then subjected to the same selective irradiation treatment, wherein the light beam is again directed onto predetermined portions to induce sintering or melting, followed by solidification. This sequence of powder-layer deposition followed by selective solidification is repeated continuously, with each new solidified layer bonding to the one beneath it. Through this iterative build-up process, the three-dimensional object gradually takes shape, layer upon layer, until the complete structure is achieved.

## Resulting Structural Features

The three-dimensional shaped object produced through this method possesses several distinctive structural characteristics that contribute to its enhanced heat removal performance. Notably, the object incorporates an internal flow path specifically designed to accommodate the circulation of cooling media, such as water or other coolant fluids. This internal channel structure allows for active thermal management during the mold's operational use, facilitating efficient heat extraction from the mold during the molding process.

Furthermore, the shaped object features a concavity-convexity surface—a surface characterized by alternating recessed and protruding regions. A significant aspect of this design is that a portion of the internal flow path's contour is configured to correspond directly with the shape of this concavity-convexity surface. This intentional correlation between the internal cooling channel geometry and the external or internal surface topology ensures that the cooling media flows in close proximity to critical surface areas, maximizing the efficiency of heat transfer and thereby optimizing the overall thermal management capabilities of the mold. This structural relationship between the flow path and the textured surface represents a key innovation that distinguishes this manufacturing method from conventional mold production techniques, enabling the creation of cooling systems that are intimately integrated with the mold's functional surface geometry.

# Method for Manufacturing a Three-Dimensional Shaped Object

## Technical Field

The present invention relates to a method for manufacturing a three-dimensional shaped object, and more particularly to a manufacturing technique suitable for producing metal molds having enhanced heat removal characteristics. The invention addresses the persistent challenge in mold-making technology of achieving efficient thermal management within dies and molds used in injection molding, die casting, and similar manufacturing processes.

## Background

Conventional metal molds typically incorporate cooling channels formed through conventional drilling or machining operations. These traditional approaches impose significant geometric constraints, generally limiting cooling passages to straight-line paths or simple geometric configurations. Consequently, the cooling media flow paths in such molds often fail to closely follow the contours of the molding surface, particularly in regions featuring complex three-dimensional geometries, undercuts, or intricate surface patterns. This mismatch between the cooling channel geometry and the actual mold surface topology results in uneven heat distribution, localized hot spots, extended cooling cycle times, and ultimately reduced production efficiency and inconsistent product quality.

## Summary of the Method

The manufacturing method disclosed herein employs an additive manufacturing approach based on powder-bed fusion technology. The process proceeds through the following repeated sequence of operations:

**Step 1: Powder-Layer Formation**
A layer of metal powder material is deposited across a build platform or previously formed layer to a predetermined, uniform thickness. This powder layer serves as the raw material from which each cross-sectional slice of the three-dimensional object will be formed.

**Step 2: Selective Light-Beam Irradiation**
A light beam—which may comprise a laser beam, electron beam, or other suitable high-energy directed radiation source—is selectively directed onto predetermined portions of the powder layer corresponding to the cross-sectional shape of the object at that particular height. The irradiated regions of powder are thereby sintered or melted, and upon cooling, solidify to form a solid layer that is metallurgically bonded to the layer beneath it.

**Step 3: Repetition and Layer Stacking**
Steps 1 and 2 are repeated in alternating cycles, with each new powder layer formed atop the previously solidified layer. Through this successive lamination process, the three-dimensional shaped object is gradually built up, layer by layer, until the complete geometry of the intended mold is achieved.

## Key Structural Feature: Contour-Following Cooling Channels

A distinguishing characteristic of the three-dimensional shaped object produced by this method is the internal cooling media flow path formed within the object during the layer-by-layer fabrication process. Because the additive manufacturing technique allows for essentially unrestricted control over the shape and path of solidified material at each layer, the internal flow path can be designed and formed with a contour surface that closely mirrors—and indeed shares substantially the same shape as—the concavity-convexity surface pattern present on the external molding surface of the object.

In other words, rather than being confined to straight or simple curved channels bearing no particular relationship to the mold's surface geometry, the cooling channel is shaped to trace the undulations, projections, and recesses of the mold cavity surface itself. Where the mold surface exhibits a convex projection, the underlying cooling channel likewise follows a correspondingly convex path at a substantially uniform depth beneath that surface; where the mold surface exhibits a concave depression, the cooling channel follows a correspondingly concave path.

## Advantages

By maintaining a substantially constant distance between the cooling channel wall and the mold surface—even across geometrically complex regions—this configuration achieves several significant benefits:

1. **Uniform Heat Extraction**: Since the cooling media flows at a consistent proximity to the molding surface throughout the entire contour, heat generated during the molding process (such as from injected molten resin or metal) is removed more uniformly across the entire mold surface, eliminating localized hot spots that would otherwise occur in regions distant from a conventional straight-line cooling channel.

2. **Reduced Cooling Cycle Time**: The improved efficiency of heat removal shortens the time required for the molded product to cool and solidify sufficiently for ejection, thereby increasing overall production throughput.

3. **Improved Product Quality**: More uniform thermal conditions across the mold surface reduce the incidence of warping, sink marks, residual stress, and other defects in molded products that arise from uneven cooling.

4. **Design Freedom**: The additive, layer-by-layer nature of the manufacturing process liberates mold designers from the geometric limitations inherent in conventional subtractive channel-forming methods, enabling cooling channels to be routed through previously inaccessible regions of the mold, including deep cavities, thin ribs, and other complex features.

Through this method, therefore, a three-dimensional shaped object suitable for use as a high-performance metal mold can be efficiently manufactured, one which achieves markedly superior thermal management compared to molds produced by conventional machining techniques.

# Patent Abstract

**Title:** Method for Manufacturing Three-Dimensional Shaped Objects with Internal Cooling Channels Using Powder-Layer Sintering and Light Beam Solidification

**Abstract:**

A method for manufacturing three-dimensional shaped metal objects incorporating internal cooling channels is disclosed, particularly suited for the production of metal molds used in injection molding, die casting, and similar applications. The method comprises depositing successive thin layers of metallic powder material onto a work surface, followed by selective irradiation of each layer with a focused light beam, such as a laser, to induce localized sintering or melting and subsequent solidification of the powder in accordance with cross-sectional data derived from a three-dimensional digital model of the desired object. By repeating the steps of powder deposition and selective beam-induced solidification layer by layer, a solid three-dimensional structure is progressively built up, wherein predetermined regions corresponding to each cross-section are left unsolidified or are shaped to define continuous internal cavities. These cavities form conformal cooling channels that follow the contour of the mold surface, enabling cooling media to circulate through the interior of the finished mold in close proximity to the molding surface. The resulting mold structure achieves more uniform and efficient heat dissipation during use compared to conventionally drilled straight-line cooling channels, thereby reducing cycle times, minimizing thermal distortion, and improving the dimensional accuracy and surface quality of molded parts. The disclosed method further allows for the integral formation of complex channel geometries—including curved, branched, and variable cross-section passages—that would be difficult or impossible to produce using traditional subtractive machining techniques, while simultaneously fabricating the surrounding mold body as a unified, dense metallic structure suitable for direct use or minimal post-processing in industrial mold-making applications.

# PATENT SPECIFICATION SUMMARY

## Title
**LAYER-BY-LAYER ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING PROCESS FOR FABRICATING MOLDS WITH INTEGRATED CONFORMAL COOLING CHANNELS**

---

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a method of manufacturing molds used in injection molding, blow molding, die casting, and related forming processes, and more particularly to a layer-by-layer additive manufacturing process for producing a mold body having a cooling media flow path formed integrally within the mold and configured to conform to a concave-convex (undulating) surface pattern of the mold cavity.

---

## Background of the Invention

Conventional molds having cooling channels are typically manufactured by drilling straight bore holes through a solid mold block. Because drilling produces only linear channel geometry, the resulting cooling paths cannot follow the contour of a molding surface that includes complex concave-convex (wavy, ribbed, or textured) features. Consequently, regions of the mold corresponding to convex protrusions or deep concave recesses experience non-uniform distances from the cooling channel to the molding surface, resulting in uneven heat extraction, extended cooling cycle times, warpage, sink marks, and reduced product quality. Existing conformal-cooling approaches employing multi-piece channel inserts, brazed channel halves, or bent tubing suffer from limitations including channel leakage at joints, dimensional inaccuracy, restricted channel geometries, and increased manufacturing cost and lead time. There remains a need for a fabrication method capable of producing a unitary mold structure with an internal cooling flow path whose depth and geometry conform locally to a concave-convex molding surface, thereby achieving substantially uniform wall thickness between the flow path and the molding surface across the entire mold.

---

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides a layer-by-layer additive manufacturing process for fabricating a mold having a molding surface that defines a concave-convex (uneven) surface pattern, and a cooling media flow path formed within the mold body such that the flow path itself follows a corresponding concave-convex path substantially parallel to, and offset by a predetermined distance from, the molding surface.

The process generally comprises:

1. **Data Preparation** — generating three-dimensional shape data of the mold including the concave-convex molding surface pattern and a corresponding flow-path pattern derived by offsetting the molding surface data by a predetermined wall-thickness distance;

2. **Slicing** — dividing the three-dimensional shape data into a plurality of two-dimensional cross-sectional layers, each layer containing data representing (a) a molding-surface-forming region, (b) a flow-path region (to remain hollow or to be filled with a fugitive/sacrificial material), and (c) a solid mold-body-forming region;

3. **Layer Formation** — sequentially forming each cross-sectional layer by selectively solidifying a raw material (metal powder, resin, or other solidifiable material) according to the sliced layer data, using an energy beam (laser or electron beam), binder deposition, or equivalent additive technique;

4. **Flow Path Formation** — during layer formation, leaving a hollow region corresponding to the flow-path cross section unsolidified (or filling it with removable support/sacrificial material) at each layer, such that as layers accumulate, the hollow regions interconnect to form a continuous three-dimensional cooling channel following the concave-convex contour;

5. **Repetition and Stacking** — repeating steps 3–4 for successive layers until the mold body, the molding surface, and the enclosed flow path are completed in their entirety; and

6. **Post-Processing** — optionally removing sacrificial fill material from the flow path, and performing finishing operations (surface machining, polishing, heat treatment) on the molding surface as needed, without disturbing the internal flow path geometry.

Because the flow-path cross-sectional data at each layer is generated as a geometric offset of the corresponding molding-surface data, the resulting cooling channel automatically replicates the concave-convex undulation of the molding surface at a substantially constant standoff distance. This enables uniform heat transfer across peaks, valleys, and transitional regions of the mold, reducing cycle time and improving dimensional consistency of molded products, while avoiding the joint-related leakage and assembly inaccuracies associated with multi-piece conformal cooling inserts.

---

## Brief Description of the Drawings

- **FIG. 1** — Perspective view of a mold having a concave-convex molding surface with an internal cooling flow path.
- **FIG. 2** — Cross-sectional view illustrating the flow path formed parallel to the concave-convex surface pattern.
- **FIG. 3** — Flow diagram of the layer-by-layer additive manufacturing process.
- **FIG. 4** — Sequential cross-sectional views showing successive layer formation and flow-path hollow-region interconnection.
- **FIG. 5** — Schematic of the offset-based data generation method for deriving flow-path geometry from molding-surface geometry.

---

## Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments

### A. Mold Structure

The mold comprises a mold body having a first surface (the molding surface) exhibiting a repeating or irregular concave-convex pattern (e.g., ribs, dimples, lens structures, or textured panel surfaces), and a cooling media flow path disposed within the mold body. The flow path has an inlet and outlet for circulation of a cooling (or heating) medium such as water, oil, or gas, and is positioned such that the shortest distance from any point on the flow path to the corresponding nearest point on the molding surface remains substantially constant, within a predetermined tolerance, across the entire mold.

### B. Data Generation

Three-dimensional CAD data representing the molding surface is obtained. A flow-path surface is generated by offsetting the molding surface data inward (into the mold body) by a designated distance corresponding to a desired mold wall thickness. The flow-path surface is then thickened or extruded to a designated channel diameter/cross section to define the three-dimensional volume of the cooling flow path. This composite data set — comprising the mold-body-forming region, the molding-surface-forming region, and the flow-path region — is supplied to a slicing module.

### C. Layer-by-Layer Formation

The slicing module divides the composite three-dimensional data into a stack of two-dimensional layer data sets, each corresponding to a layer thickness suited to the additive manufacturing apparatus employed (e.g., 20–100 micrometers for powder-bed fusion). For each layer:

- Raw material (e.g., metal powder) is deposited across a build platform;
- An energy beam selectively solidifies the material in regions corresponding to the mold body and molding surface for that layer, per the sliced data;
- The region corresponding to the flow-path cross section is left unsolidified, or is filled with a removable sacrificial material (e.g., soluble support material, low-melting-point alloy, or powder later removed via evacuation) to provide structural support for subsequent layers;
- The build platform is indexed downward (or the recoater indexed upward) by one layer thickness, and the process is repeated.

As successive layers are formed, the unsolidified/sacrificial regions of each layer align and interconnect vertically and laterally to define a continuous, unobstructed three-dimensional flow path within the finished mold body, without requiring subsequent joining, brazing, or insertion of separate channel-defining components.

### D. Post-Processing

Upon completion of the build, loose powder or sacrificial fill material is removed from the flow path (e.g., by pressurized fluid evacuation, chemical dissolution, or thermal removal), leaving an open channel. The molding surface may undergo secondary finishing (machining, EDM, polishing) to achieve final surface tolerance and texture, while the internal flow-path geometry remains protected and undisturbed by virtue of its enclosed, sub-surface location.

### E. Alternative Embodiments

Alternative embodiments include: (i) forming multiple parallel or branching flow paths conforming to different regions of a complex molding surface; (ii) varying the offset distance and/or channel cross-sectional area locally to tailor heat extraction rates to specific mold regions; (iii) employing multiple raw materials within a single build to combine high-thermal-conductivity mold-body regions with structural regions; and (iv) integrating temperature sensor channels or additional fluid paths (e.g., for mold-heating cycles) using the same layer-by-layer offset methodology.

---

## Claims (Representative)

1. A method of manufacturing a mold, comprising: generating three-dimensional data representing a molding surface having a concave-convex pattern and a mold body; generating flow-path data by offsetting the molding surface data by a predetermined distance; slicing the combined data into a plurality of layer data sets; and sequentially forming the mold body layer by layer according to the layer data sets, such that a cooling media flow path is formed within the mold body substantially conforming to the concave-convex pattern of the molding surface.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein forming each layer comprises selectively solidifying a raw material using an energy beam while leaving a region corresponding to the flow path unsolidified.

3. The method of claim 1, further comprising filling the flow-path region with a removable sacrificial material during layer formation and subsequently removing the sacrificial material after completion of the mold body.

4. The method of claim 1, wherein the predetermined distance is substantially constant across the molding surface, such that a wall thickness between the flow path and the molding surface is substantially uniform.

5. The method of claim 1, wherein the raw material comprises a metal powder and the layers are formed by powder-bed fusion.

6. A mold produced by the method of claim 1.

---

*[End of Summary — full specification to include additional claims, detailed drawings, and enablement disclosure as required by applicable patent office regulations.]*

# Method for Manufacturing a Metal Mold Having Internal Cooling Channels Using Layered Powder Solidification

## Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to a method for manufacturing a metal mold, and more particularly to a method for producing a three-dimensional metal mold body having internal cooling channels formed therein through the alternating deposition of powder layers and the selective solidification thereof by irradiation with a light beam, thereby improving heat removal characteristics of the mold during a molding operation.

---

## Background

In conventional metal mold manufacturing, cooling channels are typically formed by mechanical drilling or by joining separately machined mold segments. Such conventional approaches present limitations in that cooling channels can only be formed along linear paths, or complex assembly and sealing structures are required, resulting in insufficient heat removal efficiency in regions of the mold distant from a cooling channel. Consequently, uneven cooling of a molded article occurs, leading to defects such as warpage, sink marks, and prolonged cycle times.

Accordingly, there exists a need for a manufacturing method capable of forming cooling channels of arbitrary three-dimensional configuration in close conformity with a mold cavity surface, so as to achieve substantially uniform heat removal throughout the mold.

---

## Summary of the Invention

According to one aspect, there is provided a method for manufacturing a metal mold, comprising:

**(a)** a powder layer forming step of depositing a layer of metal powder onto a base member or onto a previously solidified layer, so as to form a powder layer having a predetermined thickness;

**(b)** a solidified layer forming step of irradiating a predetermined region of the powder layer with a light beam so as to sinter or melt the metal powder within said predetermined region, thereby forming a solidified layer bonded to an underlying layer; and

**(c)** repeating the powder layer forming step and the solidified layer forming step alternately, a plurality of times, so as to stack the solidified layers one upon another and thereby build up a three-dimensional shaped body constituting the metal mold,

wherein, in at least one of the repetitions, the predetermined region irradiated with the light beam is set so as to leave a non-irradiated region corresponding to a cross-sectional shape of a cooling channel, whereby the non-irradiated region of unsolidified powder is left in the shaped body at a location corresponding to the cooling channel, and

wherein, after completion of the stacking, the unsolidified powder remaining in the non-irradiated region is removed from the shaped body, thereby forming a hollow cooling channel extending through an interior of the metal mold along a three-dimensional path.

By this configuration, the cooling channel can be formed so as to follow a curved or branched path conforming to the shape of a cavity surface of the metal mold, rather than being restricted to a linear path as in conventional drilling methods, whereby heat generated during a molding operation can be removed substantially uniformly from the vicinity of the cavity surface, and thereby cooling irregularities in a molded article can be suppressed.

---

## Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments

### Overall Configuration

Referring to the drawings, a mold manufacturing apparatus suitable for carrying out the present method comprises: a powder supply unit configured to supply metal powder onto a base plate or a work table; a recoater or squeegee member configured to spread the supplied metal powder so as to form a powder layer of substantially uniform thickness; a light beam irradiation unit, such as a laser irradiation device or an electron beam irradiation device, configured to selectively irradiate the powder layer according to slice data derived from a three-dimensional model of the metal mold; and a control unit configured to control the powder supply unit, the recoater, and the light beam irradiation unit in accordance with the slice data so as to execute the alternating layer-forming and solidifying steps described above.

### Powder Layer Forming Step

In the powder layer forming step, metal powder, such as iron-based powder, maraging steel powder, stainless steel powder, or other alloy powder suited for mold applications, is deposited so as to form a powder layer having a thickness in a range of, for example, 0.02 mm to 0.1 mm, although the thickness is not limited thereto and may be set as appropriate depending on required dimensional accuracy and productivity.

### Solidified Layer Forming Step

In the solidified layer forming step, the control unit causes the light beam irradiation unit to scan the light beam over the powder layer according to a two-dimensional cross-sectional pattern obtained by slicing a three-dimensional model of the mold, including the cooling channel, at a predetermined pitch corresponding to the layer thickness. The light beam irradiation raises the temperature of the metal powder within the irradiated region to a temperature sufficient to sinter or melt the powder particles, such that the powder particles fuse to one another and to the solidified layer therebeneath, thereby forming an integrally bonded solidified layer.

Notably, in cross-sectional patterns corresponding to a region through which the cooling channel is to extend, the light beam irradiation unit is controlled so as **not** to irradiate the region corresponding to the cross section of the cooling channel, or is controlled to irradiate only a peripheral boundary region thereof so as to form a wall portion defining the cooling channel, while leaving an internal region thereof as unsolidified powder.

### Formation of Three-Dimensional Cooling Channel

By repeating the above steps while progressively shifting the position and cross-sectional shape of the non-irradiated region in accordance with the three-dimensional path of the intended cooling channel, it becomes possible to form a cooling channel having a curved portion, a branched portion, a portion of varying cross-sectional diameter, or a portion disposed so as to conform closely to a contour of a cavity-defining surface of the metal mold, at a substantially constant distance therefrom. This configuration is not achievable by conventional gun-drilling techniques, which are restricted to straight-line channels.

### Removal of Unsolidified Powder

After completion of the stacking of all solidified layers so as to form the shaped body constituting the metal mold, the unsolidified powder remaining within the non-irradiated region is discharged from the shaped body, for example, through an opening communicating with the cooling channel, such as by application of compressed air, vibration, suction, or a combination thereof. As a result, a hollow cooling channel is formed within the interior of the metal mold.

### Optional Additional Steps

Optionally, the method may further comprise a step of subjecting the shaped body to a post-processing treatment, such as a hot isostatic pressing treatment, a heat treatment, a machining treatment of a cavity surface, or a surface finishing treatment, after the stacking step and the powder removal step.

Optionally, the light beam irradiation unit may be configured to vary an irradiation condition, such as a laser output, a scanning speed, or a beam spot diameter, between a region corresponding to an outer contour of the metal mold and a region corresponding to a wall portion defining the cooling channel, so as to control a surface roughness of an inner wall surface of the cooling channel independently of a surface roughness of an outer surface of the metal mold.

---

## Advantageous Effects

According to the above-described method, since the cooling channel is formed integrally with the mold body through the layered powder solidification process, it becomes possible to dispose the cooling channel so as to conform to the three-dimensional contour of the cavity surface, thereby achieving substantially uniform cooling of a molded article, shortening a molding cycle time, and suppressing molding defects attributable to uneven cooling, as compared with conventional mechanically drilled cooling channels restricted to linear configurations.

---

*Note: This draft is intended as a stylistic template for patent-style disclosure language. Claims, specific numerical ranges, and drawing references should be tailored to the actual invention, prior art landscape, and jurisdictional requirements (e.g., USPTO, EPO, JPO formatting conventions) before filing.*

# Patent Claim

**Claim 1**

A method for manufacturing a metal mold by three-dimensional additive manufacturing, comprising:

acquiring three-dimensional shape data of a molding surface of the metal mold, the molding surface having a concavo-convex configuration corresponding to a product shape to be molded;

generating, based on the three-dimensional shape data of the molding surface, cooling flow path design data defining a cooling flow path to be formed inside the metal mold, wherein the cooling flow path design data is generated such that a contour line of the cooling flow path, in a cross-section taken parallel to the molding surface, is configured to follow the concavo-convex configuration of the molding surface, so that a distance between the cooling flow path and the molding surface is maintained substantially constant across a convex portion, a concave portion, and a flat portion of the molding surface; and

forming the metal mold by successively laminating a plurality of metal powder layers based on the three-dimensional shape data of the molding surface and the cooling flow path design data, each of the metal powder layers being selectively melted and solidified by irradiation with a laser beam or an electron beam according to a cross-sectional shape of the metal mold at a corresponding lamination height, thereby integrally forming the molding surface having the concavo-convex configuration and the cooling flow path having the contour line following the concavo-convex configuration within a single continuous metal body,

wherein the cooling flow path is formed as a three-dimensional path having a curved portion that rises along the convex portion of the molding surface and a curved portion that recedes along the concave portion of the molding surface, such that a wall thickness between the cooling flow path and the molding surface is substantially uniform over an entire area of the molding surface, thereby enhancing heat dissipation efficiency during molding operation of the metal mold.

---

**Claim 2** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, wherein the distance between the cooling flow path and the molding surface is maintained within a range of 3 mm to 15 mm along an entirety of the contour line following the concavo-convex configuration.

**Claim 3** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, wherein the generating of the cooling flow path design data comprises calculating a normal vector at a plurality of points on the molding surface, and defining a corresponding plurality of points on the cooling flow path by offsetting each of the plurality of points on the molding surface along the corresponding normal vector by a predetermined offset distance.

**Claim 4** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, wherein the cooling flow path comprises a plurality of branch passages, and wherein the plurality of metal powder layers are laminated such that the plurality of branch passages are formed at different lamination heights so as to be distributed along the concavo-convex configuration of the molding surface in a thickness direction of the metal mold.

**Claim 5** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, wherein an inner wall surface of the cooling flow path is formed, during the forming of the metal mold, with a surface roughness different from a surface roughness of the molding surface, by adjusting at least one of a laser output, a scanning speed, and a scanning pitch used in the irradiation with the laser beam or the electron beam.

**Claim 6** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, further comprising forming, integrally with the metal mold by the successively laminating of the plurality of metal powder layers, a plurality of support ribs connecting an inner wall of the cooling flow path and a region of the metal mold surrounding the cooling flow path, at intervals along a longitudinal direction of the cooling flow path.

**Claim 7** (dependent)

The method according to claim 1, wherein the metal powder comprises at least one selected from the group consisting of maraging steel powder, stainless steel powder, and a cobalt-chromium alloy powder, and wherein the forming of the metal mold further comprises performing a heat treatment on the laminated metal body after the successively laminating of the plurality of metal powder layers is completed.

# METHOD AND APPARATUS FOR MANUFACTURING SHAPED ARTICLES WITH CONTOUR-FOLLOWING COOLANT CHANNELS BY SELECTIVE LAYER SOLIDIFICATION

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates to methods and apparatus for the layer-by-layer manufacture of three-dimensional shaped articles from powdered material by selectively sintering or melting successive layers of powder using a directed energy beam. More particularly, the invention relates to a process for producing tooling components, such as injection mold inserts, die casting tools, blow mold segments, and similar shaped articles, in which internal coolant or heating medium channels are formed integrally within the body of the article during the build process, the channels being disposed at a substantially constant depth beneath, and following the contour of, an exterior working surface having a complex, non-planar, or freeform geometry.

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Tooling components used in injection molding, die casting, blow molding, and similar forming processes frequently possess working surfaces of complex, curved, or otherwise non-planar contour, dictated by the geometry of the part to be formed. During the forming operation, it is often necessary to remove heat rapidly and uniformly from the working surface, or in some instances to supply heat thereto, in order to control the solidification or curing rate of the material being formed, to reduce cycle time, and to achieve uniform part quality free of warpage, sink marks, or other defects attributable to non-uniform thermal history.

Conventional tooling is typically manufactured by machining a solid block of tool steel or other suitable material, followed by the drilling of straight cooling channels (commonly termed "conformal cooling" when contoured, or simply "cooling lines" when straight) from one or more faces of the block. Because conventional drilling operations are constrained to substantially straight-line paths, the resulting cooling channels cannot readily follow the contour of a complex, curved, or undulating working surface. Consequently, in regions where the working surface is deeply recessed, sharply curved, or otherwise deviates substantially from planarity, the drilled cooling channel is necessarily located at a distance from the working surface that varies significantly along the surface, sometimes being positioned quite close to the surface and at other locations quite far removed from it.

This non-uniform spacing between the cooling channel and the working surface results in non-uniform heat transfer rates across the surface, producing localized hot spots and cold spots on the tool. Such thermal non-uniformity, in turn, produces corresponding non-uniformity in the quality, dimensional accuracy, and cycle time of parts formed against the tool. Attempts have been made to intersect multiple straight-drilled channels, to employ baffles, bubblers, and similar inserts, or to use beryllium-copper alloy inserts having higher thermal conductivity in localized regions, in order to compensate for the inherent limitations of straight-line drilling. These approaches add considerable cost and complexity to tool manufacture and provide, at best, an imperfect approximation of true contour-following cooling.

More recently, so-called "conformal cooling" tooling has been proposed, in which cooling channels are designed, by means of computer-aided design software, to follow the contour of the working surface at a substantially constant depth therebeneath. However, channels of this design generally cannot be produced by conventional machining or drilling techniques, and instead require some form of additive or layer-based manufacturing process, such as selective laser sintering, direct metal laser sintering, electron beam melting, or a similar powder-bed fusion process, in order to be realized in practice.

There remains a need in the art for an improved method of manufacturing shaped articles, particularly tooling components, in which internal channels for the circulation of a coolant or heating medium are formed integrally with the body of the article, following the contour of an exterior surface of arbitrarily complex geometry at a substantially uniform standoff distance, and for apparatus suitable for carrying out such a method.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with the present invention, there is provided a method of manufacturing a shaped article from a particulate material, comprising the steps of depositing a first layer of particulate material upon a support, directing a beam of energy onto selected portions of the first layer so as to sinter, fuse, or melt the particulate material in the selected portions and thereby form a first solidified layer corresponding to a first cross-section of the article, depositing a second layer of particulate material upon the first solidified layer, directing the beam of energy onto selected portions of the second layer so as to form a second solidified layer corresponding to a second cross-section of the article, and repeating the steps of depositing and selectively solidifying successive layers of particulate material until the article is completed.

According to a principal aspect of the invention, the selected portions of at least some of the successive layers which are solidified are determined such that the solidified layers collectively define, within the interior of the completed article, at least one continuous channel for the passage of a coolant or heating fluid, the channel being disposed at a depth beneath an exterior working surface of the article which remains substantially constant along the length of the channel, notwithstanding that the exterior working surface itself may exhibit a curved, undulating, stepped, or otherwise non-planar and non-uniform contour. In this manner, the channel itself likewise exhibits a curved, undulating, or contoured path which mirrors, or is conformal with, the contour of the exterior surface, rather than following a straight-line path as would be dictated by conventional drilling.

It is a further aspect of the invention that the cross-sectional shape and dimension of the channel may itself be varied along its length, as determined by the selective solidification of successive layers, so as to compensate for variations in the thermal mass of the article in different regions, thereby providing a further degree of control over the local rate of heat transfer between the channel and the working surface, independent of the standoff distance alone.

It is yet a further aspect of the invention that a plurality of such channels may be formed within a single article, the channels being interconnected, arranged in parallel, arranged in series, or otherwise configured, and each channel or group of channels may be provided with its own contour-following path, so as to provide independently controllable cooling or heating zones within different regions of a single tool.

The invention further provides apparatus for carrying out the above method, comprising a build chamber, a support platform vertically movable within the build chamber, a powder deposition mechanism for depositing successive layers of particulate material upon the support platform or upon previously solidified layers, a source of a directed energy beam, such as a laser or electron beam, together with beam-directing optics for scanning the beam over the surface of each deposited layer, and a control system, including a data processing unit, programmed to control the powder deposition mechanism, the beam source, and the beam-directing optics in accordance with data derived from a model of the article to be manufactured, including data defining the exterior contour of the article and data defining the desired path, depth, and cross-sectional geometry of the at least one internal channel relative to that contour.

FIG. 2 is a flow chart illustrating the principal steps of the method of the present invention.

FIG. 3 is a cross-sectional view, taken through a plurality of successive layers, of a shaped article manufactured in accordance with the present invention, illustrating an exterior surface of undulating contour and an internal channel following the contour thereof at a substantially constant depth.

FIG. 4 is a view similar to FIG. 3, illustrating an alternative embodiment in which the cross-sectional dimension of the channel varies along its length.

FIG. 5 is a schematic illustration of a plurality of independently controllable channels formed within a single article in accordance with a further embodiment of the invention.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

### Apparatus

Referring now to FIG. 1, there is shown, in schematic form, apparatus 10 suitable for carrying out the method of the present invention. The apparatus 10 comprises a build chamber 12 within which is disposed a support platform 14 mounted for vertical movement, indicated by arrow 16, by means of a suitable drive mechanism 18, such as a lead screw and stepper motor arrangement, a hydraulic or pneumatic piston, or other suitable actuator known to those skilled in the art.

A powder deposition mechanism 20 is provided for depositing successive layers 22 of a particulate material 24 upon the support platform 14, or upon previously deposited and solidified layers thereon. The powder deposition mechanism 20 may comprise, for example, a powder reservoir 26, a leveling blade or roller 28 movable across the upper surface of the support platform 14, and associated drive means (not shown in detail) for advancing the leveling blade or roller 28 across the build chamber 12 so as to deposit a layer 22 of substantially uniform thickness.

The particulate material 24 may comprise a metal powder, such as a steel powder, a stainless steel powder, a tool steel powder, a bronze-infiltrated steel powder, a nickel-based superalloy powder, or a powder of any other metal or metal alloy suitable for sintering or melting by a directed energy beam. Alternatively, the particulate material 24 may comprise a ceramic powder, a polymer powder, or a composite powder comprising a mixture of metal, ceramic, and/or polymer constituents, together with any binder materials as may be appropriate to the particular material system employed.

A source 30 of a directed energy beam 32 is disposed above the build chamber 12. The source 30 may comprise, for example, a carbon dioxide laser, a Nd:YAG laser, a fiber laser, a diode laser, or other suitable laser source, or alternatively may comprise an electron beam gun, together with associated power supplies and cooling systems as appropriate to the type of source employed.

Beam-directing optics 34, which may comprise a pair of galvanometer-driven mirrors, an acousto-optic deflector, a rotating polygon mirror, or other suitable beam-scanning means, together with a focusing lens or lens system 36, are disposed in the path of the beam 32 so as to direct the beam 32 onto selected portions of the uppermost layer 22 of particulate material 24 within the build chamber 12, and so as to scan the beam 32 across such selected portions in a desired pattern.

A control system 38, comprising a data processing unit 40, associated memory 42, and appropriate input/output interfaces 44, is operatively connected to the drive mechanism 18, the powder deposition mechanism 20, the source 30, and the beam-directing optics 34, so as to control the operation thereof in a coordinated manner in accordance with a program stored within the memory 42, as will be described in greater detail below.

Optionally, the apparatus 10 may further comprise a heating means 46, such as a resistive heating element or infrared heater, disposed so as to preheat the particulate material 24 within the build chamber 12 to a temperature below its melting or sintering point, so as to reduce thermal gradients and associated distortion during the selective solidification process. The apparatus 10 may further comprise an inert gas supply 48 for maintaining an inert atmosphere, such as nitrogen or argon, within the build chamber 12, so as to reduce oxidation of the particulate material 24 during processing, and/or a vacuum pump (not shown) for evacuating the build chamber 12, as may be appropriate depending upon the particular particulate material 24 employed.
